items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 士 as a single sword driven straight into the mossy step at the shrine, blade down, hilt up. One crossguard sits high and long, marking rank; a shorter belt-line crosses near the base. It never wavers, never leans — that stillness alone is what makes a <kanji>gentleman</kanji>, a scholar, a <radical>samurai</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine, cats keep grooming against his rigid shin, mistaking him for another statue. He never moves — just hisses a flat, warning <reading>し</reading>, like <reading>sheesh</reading> through his teeth, and the cats scatter.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の兄は弁護士です。
example_sentences.english: My older brother is a lawyer.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の兄[あに]は弁[べん]護[ご]士[し]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あの消防士は親切です。
example_sentences.english: That firefighter is kind.
example_sentences.furigana: あの消[しょう]防[ぼう]士[し]は親[しん]切[せつ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 弁護士は毎日忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: The lawyer is busy every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 弁[べん]護[ご]士[し]は毎[まい]日[にち]忙[いそが]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 謝 as one arrow of <radical>words</radical> shot clean across the riverbank, landing point-down at someone's feet instead of in their chest. Whoever fired it bends their whole <radical>body</radical> into a bow, measuring the distance to a single <radical>inch</radical>, hands empty, message delivered. That is how you <kanji>apologize</kanji>: words aimed to land soft, not to wound.
items.reading_mnemonic: The archer at the riverbank, a title everyone shortens to <reading>Shah</reading>, still cannot fire a straight shot. Every arrow that misses gets the same muttered <reading>しゃ</reading>, half apology, half excuse, as he bows and fishes it out of the reeds.
items.description: This kanji covers more than sorry: the same character also carries formal thanks and, in some compounds, an outright refusal or decline. Underneath all three is one idea, a formal spoken response rather than plain regret, so context decides whether it reads as apology, gratitude, or a firm no.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は友達にすぐ謝った。
example_sentences.english: I apologized to my friend right away.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]にすぐ謝[あやま]った。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は先生に感謝しています。
example_sentences.english: He is grateful to his teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は先[せん]生[せい]に感[かん]謝[しゃ]しています。

example_sentences.japanese: 私はいつも家族に感謝しています。
example_sentences.english: I'm always grateful to my family.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はいつも家[か]族[ぞく]に感[かん]謝[しゃ]しています。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The riverbank that should be rushing with water is nothing but a maze of cracked, <radical>sun</radical>-baked mud plates. Each crack forms a stray <radical>chevron</radical> mark, and the deepest fissures cross into a perfect <radical>cross</radical>. A heron stands in the middle on one leg, unable to remember what wet ground felt like. The whole bank has gone bone dry — a total <kanji>drought</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The same heron kicks an empty tin <reading>can</reading> across the cracked mud out of pure boredom. It rolls to a stop with a hollow <reading>かん</reading> — the only sound this drought-cracked riverbank makes all summer.

example_sentences.japanese: この服はまだ乾いていません。
example_sentences.english: These clothes aren't dry yet.
example_sentences.furigana: この服[ふく]はまだ乾[かわ]いていません。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は毎朝髪を乾かします。
example_sentences.english: He dries his hair every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]髪[かみ]を乾[かわ]かします。

example_sentences.japanese: タオルを窓の近くに置いて乾かしましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's put the towel near the window to dry it.
example_sentences.furigana: タオルを窓[まど]の近[ちか]くに置[お]いて乾[かわ]かしましょう。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail the steep path suddenly flattens into a clearing. Rows of square rice paddies stack neatly on a thick slab of packed earth. The whole grid sits there through every season without shifting. Hikers stop, catch their breath, and realize they've stumbled straight into a <radical>village</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The village elder who waves hikers toward the paddies goes by <reading>Lee</reading>. Every exhausted hiker calls back a grateful <reading>り</reading> as thanks. That's as much of his name as anyone manages out of breath. He just nods toward the shade.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer draws a long blade to slice open a stubborn onigiri wrapper. It sweeps down and hooks sharp at the tip, but the plastic fights back and chips a nick right at the top edge. Everyone stares at the scratched blade: an actual <radical>sword</radical>, ruined on rice packaging.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clerk points and yells <reading>とう</reading>, sounding just like someone stubbing a <reading>toe</reading> on the counter, before confiscating the blade for scratching the onigiri shelf.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer plants one <radical>hand</radical> flat on the last onigiri, elbow cocked out like a <radical>halberd</radical> guarding it. He shoots the whole line a <radical>barb</radical>ed glare. He mutters that the shelf, the till, and the entire store were built for him. Nobody else gets within an arm's length of it. That elbows-out glare is pure <kanji>ego</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The staff have nicknamed him <reading>Gah</reading>. Every time a hand drifts toward his onigiri, he barks <reading>が</reading> without even looking up, elbows still locked around the shelf.
items.description: As a stand-alone word, 我 (われ) is formal and literary — it isn't how someone says "I" in an ordinary conversation. Day to day it survives mostly inside set compounds about endurance and self rather than standing alone.

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は公園で怪我しました。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother got injured at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は公[こう]園[えん]で怪[け]我[が]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 足の怪我はもう大丈夫ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is your leg injury already all right?
example_sentences.furigana: 足[あし]の怪[け]我[が]はもう大[だい]丈[じょう]夫[ぶ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 頭を怪我して、病院に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I hurt my head and went to the hospital.
example_sentences.furigana: 頭[あたま]を怪[け]我[が]して、病[びょう]院[いん]に行[い]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a fat cat leaps onto the bell rope, snagging her <radical>clothing</radical> sleeve as it swings. The rope snaps, and the enormous bell tears free. It thunders down the mossy steps and buries itself in the bare <radical>earth</radical> below, cracking a <radical>cross</radical> of broken stone where it lands. Grandma Kane just sighs — she'll have to <radical>buy</radical> a new bell. Another Tuesday of <kanji>demolition</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's apprentice, a boy named <reading>Kai</reading>, surveys the wreckage and sighs the count out loud: <reading>かい</reading> — the third bell disaster this year alone. He says it flat, already reaching for the broom.

example_sentences.japanese: 弟が私の時計を壊した。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother broke my watch.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]が私[わたし]の時計[とけい]を壊[こわ]した。

example_sentences.japanese: パソコンが壊れた。
example_sentences.english: The computer broke.
example_sentences.furigana: パソコンが壊[こわ]れた。

example_sentences.japanese: 誰が窓を壊しましたか。
example_sentences.english: Who broke the window?
example_sentences.furigana: 誰[だれ]が窓[まど]を壊[こわ]しましたか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: See 提 as one rigid <radical>hand</radical>, elbow locked, fingers wrapped around a briefcase handle, thrust straight across Koichi's counter under the fluorescent <radical>sun</radical>-bright lights. It's not a purchase, it's a pitch. The clerk's <radical>head</radical> doesn't even lift from ringing up the bento. That raised hand, holding a whole idea out for someone else to take, is <kanji>propose</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Tei, a deer too formal for the konbini, holds an empty tray at arm's length over that same counter like he's presenting a proposal, and repeats <reading>てい</reading>, <reading>tray</reading>, until someone puts something on it. Nobody ever does; he holds the pose anyway.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は宿題を提出した。
example_sentences.english: I submitted my homework.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]を提[てい]出[しゅつ]した。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は会社に書類提出をした。
example_sentences.english: He submitted documents to the company.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は会[かい]社[しゃ]に書[しょ]類[るい]提[てい]出[しゅつ]をした。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達は旅行を提案した。
example_sentences.english: My friend proposed a trip.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]は旅[りょ]行[こう]を提[てい]案[あん]した。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, the archery club lines up their weapons, stacked curves of springy wood bent back on themselves, notched at both ends where the string bites in. A coach pulls one taut until it hums, holding a <radical>bow</radical> ready to fire.
items.reading_mnemonic: A boy named <reading>Kyu</reading> lines up his shot on the sports field, and the string gives a sharp <reading>きゅう</reading> as it snaps back into place, leaving nothing but that one clean sound behind.

items.meaning_mnemonic: 頑 is a boulder shaped like a giant <radical>head</radical>, squatting dead center of the mountain trail since the trail's very <radical>beginning</radical>. A face is gouged into the granite — jaw set, eyes narrowed. Hikers heave against it, bribe it with vending-machine snacks, beg. It doesn't roll an inch. That immovable refusal is <kanji>stubborn</kanji>, plain and simple.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every time a hiker shoves the boulder, a hermit camped beside it cups his hands and grunts <reading>がん</reading> — the same flat sound, like someone saying <reading>gone</reading> through a clenched jaw. It's the only word he says. The boulder still hasn't moved.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は毎日仕事を頑張っています。
example_sentences.english: He works hard at his job every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は毎[まい]日[にち]仕[し]事[ごと]を頑張[がんば]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 頑張って、テストは難しくないよ。
example_sentences.english: Do your best, the test isn't hard.
example_sentences.furigana: 頑張[がんば]って、テストは難[むずか]しくないよ。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は日本語をもっと頑張りたいです。
example_sentences.english: I want to try harder at Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は日本[にほん]語[ご]をもっと頑[がん]張[ば]りたいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 掛 as one steel hook bolted into a post sunk deep in the <radical>earth</radical> beside the mountain trail's vending machine. A <radical>hand</radical> loops a strap through it, and from that strap swings a soaked poncho and a little <radical>divination</radical> charm. It drips onto the gravel, not falling, just swaying there. One hook holding the whole poncho in midair: to <kanji>hang</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa lands on that same hook, tilts his head at the empty <reading>sky</reading>, and screeches <reading>かい</reading> at the swinging poncho. It's the same rasp he gives anything left dangling in his sightline.

example_sentences.japanese: 帽子を窓の近くに掛けた。
example_sentences.english: I hung the hat near the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 帽[ぼう]子[し]を窓[まど]の近[ちか]くに掛[か]けた。

example_sentences.japanese: 学校まで一時間掛かる。
example_sentences.english: It takes one hour to get to school.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]まで一[いち]時[じ]間[かん]掛[か]かる。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は宿題に取り掛かった。
example_sentences.english: He got started on his homework.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]に取り掛[とりか]かった。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the fair, the vendor yanks the shaft free from his ruined pumpkin. The feathers still splay at the top, the shaft still drops straight, and the point is still sharp enough to bury itself again when he flings it at the fence for fun. Now he just calls it his dart, forgetting it started as a stray <radical>arrow</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the fair, Shea guards the fence where the runaway shaft first landed. Anyone who reaches for it too fast gets a sharp <reading>し</reading> — flat, quick, cutting the sentence off like a blade through pumpkin. It sounds exactly like her name, <reading>Shea</reading>, minus the vowel.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the hot <radical>water</radical> tap for cup noodles <radical>sticks</radical> wide open, the handle bent like a drawn <radical>bow</radical>. The broth <radical>slides</radical> up past the rim in fat white bubbles. It hisses and multiplies until foam rolls off the counter and drips past the onigiri shelf. The clerk just watches it <kanji>seethe</kanji>, boil, and go faintly sour under the fluorescent lights.
items.reading_mnemonic: A jumpy regular named <reading>Futz</reading> keeps mashing the button, muttering <reading>ふつ</reading>, ふつ under his breath every time the noodle water surges past the rim. Say his nervous little ふつ ふつ and the reading is stuck in your head with the foam.

example_sentences.japanese: 姉が朝、お茶のために水を沸かします。
example_sentences.english: My sister boils water for tea in the morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 姉[あね]が朝[あさ]、お茶[ちゃ]のために水[みず]を沸[わ]かします。

example_sentences.japanese: 台所で水が沸いています。
example_sentences.english: The water is boiling in the kitchen.
example_sentences.furigana: 台[だい]所[どころ]で水[みず]が沸[わ]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は毎朝コーヒーのために水を沸かす。
example_sentences.english: I boil water for coffee every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]コーヒーのために水[みず]を沸[わ]かす。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a hooded figure crouched low to the <radical>earth</radical> behind the enormous bell at Grandma Kane's shrine at dusk. One <radical>hand</radical> hovers over the offering box, <radical>heart</radical> pounding every time a cat glances his way. Nothing about him adds up — the hood, the hovering hand, the flinching at cats. That unexplained wrongness is what <kanji>suspicious</kanji> means.
items.reading_mnemonic: The figure only gives his name as <reading>Kai</reading>, and when Grandma Kane flicks on the shrine lights without warning he yelps <reading>かい</reading> and bolts past the mossy steps, offering box completely untouched.
items.description: 怪 carries more than a raised eyebrow of doubt — it's the character behind monsters, ghost stories, and the eerie unknown, so think uncanny and unexplained before you think of doubting someone's alibi.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、公園で怪我しました。
example_sentences.english: Yesterday, I got injured at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、公[こう]園[えん]で怪[け]我[が]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は自転車で怪我しました。
example_sentences.english: My older brother got injured on his bicycle.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]で怪[け]我[が]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 頭を怪我して、病院へ行きました。
example_sentences.english: I injured my head and went to the hospital.
example_sentences.furigana: 頭[あたま]を怪[け]我[が]して、病[びょう]院[いん]へ行[い]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Three droplets flick off the wet paintbrush and splash into the <radical>water</radical> below a hot spring. A crooked roof-beam <radical>chevron</radical> lands askew on top like a hairpin. Flat layers of <radical>steam</radical> lie on the water, and the last wisp hooks up and peels into the cold — vapor rising off the pool.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit hides by the steaming pool and giggles at every gust. Cold spray hits her and she yelps <reading>き</reading>, sharp as a <reading>key</reading> turning in a lock, while the vapor drifts past her branch.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A stick of <radical>divination</radical> in the corner, a <radical>small</radical> mark beside it, a <radical>right hand</radical> scooping both up. He is the younger brother: not head of the family, so he gets the small share. Your <kanji>uncle</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shuku is that uncle, and he arrives every year with the same trick. He shuffles the sticks, throws them down, sucks his teeth, and pronounces 「<reading>しゅく</reading>」 as though it settles the matter. Nobody knows what しゅく means. He will not explain.

example_sentences.japanese: 叔父は毎週土曜日に公園で犬と遊びます。
example_sentences.english: My uncle plays with his dog in the park every Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 叔父[おじ]は毎[まい]週[しゅう]土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]で犬[いぬ]と遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 叔母は台所で魚を料理しています。
example_sentences.english: My aunt is cooking fish in the kitchen.
example_sentences.furigana: 叔母[おば]は台[だい]所[どころ]で魚[さかな]を料[りょう]理[り]しています。

example_sentences.japanese: 叔父と叔母は今日私の家に来ます。
example_sentences.english: My uncle and aunt are coming to my house today.
example_sentences.furigana: 叔父[おじ]と叔母[おば]は今日[きょう]私[わたし]の家[いえ]に来[き]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 褒 as an enormous <radical>clothing</radical> robe billowing open to wrap one <radical>small</radical> <radical>person</radical> inside it, right on the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine. Their <radical>mouth</radical> falls open in an awed little 'oh.' The cats go still, the huge bell hums instead of clangs, and the whole scene folds in soft approval. That is <kanji>praise</kanji>: wrapping someone up in it instead of striking them down.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine's caretaker, nicknamed <reading>Whoa</reading> because it's the only thing she ever says, watches the bell hum with approval. She breathes out a satisfied <reading>ほう</reading>, her robe still settling.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は私を褒めました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher praised me.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は私[わたし]を褒[ほ]めました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は宿題をして先生に褒められた。
example_sentences.english: He did his homework and was praised by the teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]をして先[せん]生[せい]に褒[ほ]められた。

example_sentences.japanese: 母はいつも妹を褒める。
example_sentences.english: My mother always praises my younger sister.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]はいつも妹[いもうと]を褒[ほ]める。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 叱 as one <radical>mouth</radical>, jaw clamped shut, with a bent <radical>spoon</radical> cracking down right beside it at Koichi's konbini. The crack knocks onigiri off the shelf and sets the till beeping. Out of that clenched mouth comes a single flat, furious <kanji>scold</kanji> that stops the whole aisle cold.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the konbini, the clerk everyone calls <reading>Sheets</reading> is still rubbing his ear from the crack of the cane. Every time the till beeps near him now, he flinches and mutters <reading>しつ</reading> under his breath, bracing for another scolding.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は弟を叱った。
example_sentences.english: My mother scolded my younger brother.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は弟[おとうと]を叱[しか]った。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生に叱られた。
example_sentences.english: I was scolded by the teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]に叱[しか]られた。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は父に叱られて泣いた。
example_sentences.english: My older brother got scolded by our father and cried.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は父[ちち]に叱[しか]られて泣[な]いた。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A customer bursts through the door of Koichi's konbini, soaked from collar to shoe. <radical>Rain</radical> sheets off him in one long trail toward the onigiri shelf. He leaves a puddle of <radical>water</radical> so deep the beeping till stutters and dies — and <radical>yet</radical> he keeps dripping. Everything about him has gotten <kanji>wet</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi mops the puddle, muttering <reading>じゅ</reading>, じゅ — it sounds exactly like the first syllable of <reading>juice</reading>, which is unfortunately also what the floor smells like now.
items.description: This character mostly means plain physical wetness — rain, tears, sweat. The "make love" sense is idiomatic, from a fixed phrase for an intimate scene in film or drama. On its own as a verb, it almost always just means damp, not romance.

example_sentences.japanese: 靴が雨で濡れました。
example_sentences.english: My shoes got wet in the rain.
example_sentences.furigana: 靴[くつ]が雨[あめ]で濡[ぬ]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は服を濡らしました。
example_sentences.english: He got his clothes wet.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は服[ふく]を濡[ぬ]らしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬が水で濡れています。
example_sentences.english: The dog is wet from the water.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]が水[みず]で濡[ぬ]れています。
